analysis.summary_en: Abstract The characterization of pathogens affecting Antarctic wildlife has been historically limited and sporadic. This study confirms avian cholera as a relevant cause of mortality in the Antarctic, and overall highlights the importance of considering this disease in the differential diagnoses during mortality events in Antarctica. By shotgun sequencing, we retrieved the first genomic sequences of the P. We detected Pasteurella multocida DNA in 46 of 49 individuals, and diagnosed avian cholera as the cause of death of most of these animals. multocida strain from this region, and the phylogenetic analysis showed a close relation with strains from other locations retrieved during the same expedition and with strains previously reported in the Southern Ocean area. With the introduction of H5N1 high pathogenicity avian influenza virus (HPAIV) in Antarctica in the austral summer 2023/2024, concerns about the health of Antarctic seabirds and mammals prompted immediate surveillance efforts. This deterministic extraction is based on retrieved fulltext evidence. The source does not explicitly report enough limitations for an independent appraisal, so confidence is low.

title: The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention response to Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1): surveillance, diagnostics, risk assessment, and public health preparedness from 1996 to 2026

analysis.scope_and_question: Avian influenza A(H5N1) remains a major zoonotic and pandemic concern because of its extensive circulation in birds, repeated spillover into mammals, and capacity to cause illness in humans ranging from asymptomatic infection or conjunctivitis to fatal pneumonia.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A structured narrative review was conducted using PubMed and authoritative sources from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), World Health Organization (WHO), Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The search covered January 1996 through 24 July 2026. Sources were screened for direct relevance and synthesized by predefined thematic domains. Table 1 presents a focused evidence map of key H5N1-specific studies and reports.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The CDC response uses surveillance systems, monitoring of exposed persons, public-health laboratory testing, rapid H5 subtyping, sequencing, antigenic characterization, and antiviral-susceptibility assessment. Human infections associated with the United States cattle and poultry outbreaks were predominantly mild and commonly involved conjunctivitis or upper-respiratory symptoms, although severe and fatal disease occurred.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Important limitations include uneven testing, incomplete participation by exposed workers, barriers to personal protective equipment use, rapidly changing surveillance data, and uncertainty regarding the frequency of mild or asymptomatic infection. The reviewed serosurveys also indicated that symptom-based surveillance can miss infections in exposed workers.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Preventive measures include occupational PPE guidance, monitoring and testing of exposed persons, infection-control recommendations, risk communication, and antiviral prophylaxis following selected high-risk exposures.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) response to avian influenza A(H5N1) from 1996 to 2026, focusing on surveillance, diagnostics, risk assessment, and pandemic preparedness. The evidence highlights the CDC's use of surveillance systems, laboratory testing, and genomic analysis to monitor H5N1 outbreaks in birds and mammals. Human infections linked to these outbreaks are mostly mild, with conjunctivitis and upper-respiratory symptoms being common, though severe cases have occurred. The review identifies key limitations, including uneven testing, incomplete worker participation, and challenges in symptom-based surveillance. It emphasizes the need for sustained One Health coordination, timely outbreak control, and continuous evaluation of viral evolution and diagnostic performance. Research and practice implications include the importance of occupational PPE guidance, worker testing, and antiviral prophylaxis for high-risk exposures.

title: Seroprevalence of Avian Influenza Viruses (H5N1 and H9N2) Among Poultry Workers and Live-Bird Market Vendors in Asia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

analysis.scope_and_question: Avian influenza A viruses, avian-origin zoonotic infections, and qualified avian subtypes. Biologically related animal, taxonomic, model, differential-diagnosis and comparative entities are supplementary-only unless material target-specific evidence is also present; only explicit lexical or unrelated hard exclusions are terminal.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: We systematically reviewed 22 studies (7 countries/territories, 26,413 participants across the 21 studies reporting sample sizes; PROSPERO: CRD420261380328).
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Using DerSimonian–Laird random-effects models with Freeman–Tukey double-arcsine transformation, pooled seroprevalence was 2.38% (95% CI 0.62–5.23%) for H5N1 (12 cohorts from 11 unique studies) and 11.79% (95% CI 5.96–19.27%) for H9N2 (13 studies).
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: South Asian H9N2 seroprevalence (24.9%; k = 4 studies) was approximately four-fold higher than that of East Asia (5.9%; k = 9 studies).
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: These findings highlight substantial, regionally uneven occupational exposure risk and an urgent need for standardized surveillance in underrepresented settings like Nepal.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis assesses the seroprevalence of avian influenza A viruses H5N1 and H9N2 among poultry workers and live-bird market vendors in Asia. The review included 22 studies from seven countries/territories, involving 26,413 participants. Pooled seroprevalence estimates were calculated using DerSimonian–Laird random-effects models with Freeman–Tukey double-arcsine transformation, yielding 2.38% (95% CI 0.62–5.23%) for H5N1 and 11.79% (95% CI 5.96–19.27%) for H9N2. Notably, H9N2 seroprevalence in South Asia was significantly higher than in East Asia, suggesting regional disparities in exposure. The findings underscore the need for standardized surveillance in underrepresented areas, such as Nepal, to better understand and mitigate occupational risks associated with avian influenza.

title: Surveillance of zoonotic avian influenza viruses H5N1 and H9N2 in selected live bird markets in Northern Nigeria: public health implications

analysis.research_question_and_background: Avian influenza viruses (AIVs), including highly pathogenic H5N1 and low pathogenic H9N2, represent significant zoonotic threats. Both subtypes have been repeatedly introduced into Nigeria since their initial detection in West Africa in 2006 and 2017, respectively.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study aimed to investigate the current genetic diversity and spillover potential of these viruses through active surveillance in live bird markets (LBMs) in Hadejia and Kano, Nigeria, from March to November 2022. We sampled 219 birds, collecting two swabs per bird (438 swab specimens).
analysis.methods: A positive bird was defined as having at least one positive swab. Phylogenetic and selection pressure analysis confirmed that the H9N2 viruses belong to the G1 lineage and harbor key mammalian adaptation signatures in the hemagglutinin (HA) gene, including S143T, S145T, and S121T, which are associated with increased affinity for human-like α2–6 sialic acid receptors.
analysis.main_results: At the bird level, highly pathogenic H5N1 was detected in 3/125 (2.4%) apparently healthy guinea fowl at Sabon Gari LBM in Kano. Notably, low pathogenic H9N2 was detected at a substantially higher prevalence, 10/94 (10.6%) in chickens at Hadejia LBM. Overall, 13/219 (5.9%) birds were positive for either H5N1 or H9N2. H5N1 and H9N2 were detected in different Nigerian live bird markets.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Although these findings do not provide evidence of current co-circulation or reassortment, the detection of both subtypes within the broader LBM system, together with putative mammalian adaptation markers in H9N2, highlights a potential reassortment risk should these viruses later co-circulate within the same market and co-infect the same host.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Continued genomic surveillance is therefore warranted to detect future viral convergence and emergent reassortant strains and to inform pandemic preparedness and control strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report on the specific statistical methods used to analyze the prevalence data, nor does it provide details on the controls or potential biases in the sampling process.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted active surveillance of avian influenza viruses H5N1 and H9N2 in live bird markets in Northern Nigeria from March to November 2022. It found that H5N1 was detected in 2.4% of guinea fowl in Kano, while H9N2 was found in 10.6% of chickens in Hadejia. Overall, 5.9% of sampled birds were positive for either virus. The H9N2 viruses were identified as belonging to the G1 lineage and showed signs of mammalian adaptation in their hemagglutinin gene. The study highlights the potential reassortment risk if these viruses co-circulate and co-infect the same host. These findings emphasize the need for continued genomic surveillance to monitor viral convergence and inform pandemic preparedness. The study's limitations include the lack of detailed statistical methods and potential biases in sampling.

title: A qualitative study exploring poultry farmers’ barriers and motivations to seasonal human influenza vaccine uptake as a preventive public health measure because of avian influenza

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore poultry farmers’ perceptions of seasonal human influenza vaccination as a preventive measure against avian influenza, given the global spread of highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) and concerns about reassortment between avian and human influenza viruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This qualitative study involved semistructured interviews with twelve poultry farmers in the Netherlands, conducted online via Microsoft Teams between June and October 2024. Participants generally perceived their personal risk of avian influenza infection as low, while acknowledging potentially severe consequences for public health if a novel influenza virus were to emerge.
analysis.methods: The study used semistructured interviews based on the attitude‒social influence‒self-efficacy (ASE) model. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed using thematic analysis. The interview guide was designed to explore perceptions and motivations related to vaccination.
analysis.main_results: Attitudes towards vaccination differed both generally and regarding seasonal influenza vaccination due to avian influenza risk. Approximately half considered vaccination a reasonable preventive measure. Accessibility was considered essential: local, flexible in timing, and free of charge.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight that vaccination acceptance among poultry farmers is influenced by a combination of societal responsibility, perceived risk, trust in the government, and practical considerations. The study identifies key motivations and barriers related to vaccine uptake in this specific group.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results can inform public health strategies by emphasizing the importance of addressing societal perceptions, trust in government, and practical accessibility when promoting seasonal influenza vaccination among poultry farmers to mitigate the risk of avian influenza reassortment.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to twelve participants, which may restrict generalisability. The evidence is based on qualitative interviews, which provide rich insights but lack quantitative data. The confidence in the findings is moderate due to the small sample size and the nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This qualitative study investigated poultry farmers’ perceptions of seasonal human influenza vaccination as a preventive measure against avian influenza, particularly in light of the global spread of H5N1. Twelve Dutch poultry farmers were interviewed between June and October 2024, using a guide based on the ASE model. The results showed that attitudes towards vaccination varied, with about half considering it a reasonable preventive measure. Key motivations included preventing reassortment between avian and human influenza viruses and reducing pandemic risk, while barriers included low perceived personal risk, distrust in government, and regulatory burdens. The study suggests that vaccination acceptance is influenced by societal responsibility, trust, and practical considerations. The findings highlight the need for vaccination programs that are accessible and tailored to farmers’ needs, with engagement from trusted intermediaries. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the small sample size and qualitative nature of the study.

title: Avian influenza A virus polymerase gene leads to temperature-resistant genome replication

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza A viruses (IAV) pose a persistent pandemic threat. Successful cross-species transmission from waterfowl to mammals requires host adaptation for efficient replication and spread.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study investigated the role of avian-origin PB1 genes in enabling IAV replication at febrile temperatures. It used a mini-replicon system and MDCK cells to compare polymerase activity of seasonal human H1N1 IAV with chimeric viruses expressing avian or pandemic-origin PB1 genes.
analysis.methods: Using a mini-replicon system, the researchers demonstrated that a seasonal human H1N1 IAV polymerase fails to replicate efficiently at 40°C, whereas substitution of the PB1 with that from pandemic viruses or a low-pathogenic avian H2N1 virus restores RNA synthesis. Activity assays with purified chimeric IAV polymerases were conducted to assess temperature-dependent replication.
analysis.main_results: Chimeric seasonal human H1N1 viruses expressing avian or 1918 PB1 replicate at 40°C in MDCK cells, unlike wild-type H1N1. Activity assays with purified chimeric IAV polymerases further suggest that avian-origin PB1 may intrinsically enhance polymerase activity at elevated temperatures.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings identify temperature-resistant genome replication as a potential adaptive property of avian-origin PB1 and suggest that acquisition of an avian PB1 may help influenza viruses overcome temperature barriers during adaptation to mammalian hosts.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Surveillance of avian-origin PB1 genes in IAVs circulating in mammals may help identify strains with pandemic potential and inform the development of countermeasures.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study provides strong evidence for the role of avian-origin PB1 in enabling IAV replication at febrile temperatures, but the findings are based on a mini-replicon system and may not fully represent in vivo conditions.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of avian-origin PB1 genes in enabling influenza A viruses (IAVs) to replicate at febrile temperatures, which is critical for cross-species transmission. Using a mini-replicon system and MDCK cells, the researchers demonstrate that avian-origin PB1 genes enhance viral RNA replication at elevated temperatures compared to seasonal human H1N1 IAV polymerases. Activity assays with purified chimeric polymerases further support this finding. The results suggest that avian-origin PB1 may provide an adaptive advantage by allowing IAVs to replicate at higher temperatures, which could facilitate zoonotic emergence and host adaptation. These findings highlight the importance of monitoring avian-origin PB1 genes in mammalian IAVs for pandemic potential. The study's evidence is strong, but its reliance on a mini-replicon system may limit its applicability to in vivo conditions.

title: Wildlife-Livestock-Human Interfaces in the Global H5N1 Panzootic: Epidemiologic Shifts and Surveillance Priorities

analysis.scope_and_question: Avian influenza A viruses, avian-origin zoonotic infections, and qualified avian subtypes. The review focuses on the epidemiologic shifts of H5N1 and other avian influenza viruses from poultry epizootics to a panzootic involving wild birds, domestic animals, and humans. The central question is how these viruses have transitioned across species and environments, and what surveillance strategies are needed.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is an expert analysis of original epidemiologic, genomic, experimental, and environmental studies. It does not report on study counts, databases, or meta-analysis. The methods section includes a case-control study of risk factors for avian influenza A (H5N1) disease in Hong Kong, 1997, and references to primary studies on clade 2.3.4.4b viruses. The review does not describe a formal meta-analysis or consensus process.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that H5N1 viruses have transitioned from poultry epizootics to a panzootic involving multiple hosts, including wild birds, domestic animals, and humans. It highlights the importance of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses in this transition, noting their ability to reach remote ecosystems and cause consequential mammalian outbreaks. The dairy-cattle emergence is emphasized due to its implications for transmission and zoonotic potential.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies gaps in understanding the mechanisms of cross-species transmission and the environmental factors that facilitate viral spread. It notes that while genomic and pathology data support the role of H5N1 in mammalian outbreaks, there is limited evidence on the full extent of its host range and the specific pathways of transmission to humans. The review also highlights the need for more comprehensive surveillance across wildlife-livestock-human interfaces.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review recommends shifting surveillance efforts toward risk-based One Health networks that integrate field observations, laboratory testing, genomic data, animal movements, and occupational health. It emphasizes the importance of early detection, faster cross-sector investigation, and rapid recognition of viral changes associated with altered host range or transmission. Environmental sampling and paired serology are suggested as complementary tools for monitoring H5N1 activity.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the epidemiologic shifts of avian influenza A(H5N1) viruses from poultry epizootics to a panzootic involving wild birds, domestic animals, and humans. It highlights the role of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses in spreading to remote ecosystems and causing mammalian outbreaks, particularly in dairy cattle. The review underscores the need for integrated surveillance strategies that combine field observations, genomic data, and environmental sampling. It identifies gaps in understanding transmission mechanisms and calls for improved cross-sector collaboration to detect and respond to viral changes. The implications emphasize the importance of risk-based One Health networks for monitoring and mitigating the spread of H5N1.

title: Biosecurity risk factors associated with outbreaks of high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) on poultry farms in Lower Saxony (Germany) – A case-control-study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to identify biosecurity risk factors associated with outbreaks of high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) on poultry farms in Lower Saxony, Germany. The background highlights that biosecurity is a critical factor in explaining why not all poultry farms are equally affected by HPAI outbreaks, despite similar environmental and operational conditions.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A case-control study was conducted in Lower Saxony, Germany, comparing 15 case farms with at least two previous HPAI outbreaks to 26 control farms without such outbreaks. The study focused on examining biosecurity measures during farm visits.
analysis.methods: During farm visits, a specially developed biosecurity checklist was used to examine 15 case farms and 26 control farms. The univariable logistic regression analysis identified several factors significantly associated with HPAI outbreak status, including longer distance to federal highways, not short-cutting grass areas around stables, lack of dedicated facilities for carcass removal, and specific storage practices for feed, litter, and manure.
analysis.main_results: In the univariable logistic regression analysis, factors such as longer distance to federal highways, not short-cutting grass areas around stables, lack of dedicated facilities for carcass removal, and feed, litter, and manure storage practices that require suppliers to enter the clean area showed significant associations with HPAI outbreak status. In the multivariable analysis, only the variables related to not short-cutting grass areas and lack of dedicated carcass removal facilities remained significant.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that specific biosecurity practices, particularly those related to grass maintenance and carcass removal, are critical in reducing the risk of HPAI outbreaks. This study provides novel insights into the operational factors that influence the spread of HPAI in poultry farms.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results can inform the development of targeted biosecurity protocols to reduce the risk of HPAI outbreaks in poultry farms, contributing to improved surveillance and prevention strategies in the poultry industry.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on self-reported data from farm visits and the potential for confounding variables. However, the use of multivariable analysis with backward stepwise regression provides a moderate level of confidence in the identified risk factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated biosecurity risk factors associated with outbreaks of high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) on poultry farms in Lower Saxony, Germany, using a case-control design. During farm visits, a biosecurity checklist was employed to assess 15 case farms with multiple HPAI outbreaks against 26 control farms without such outbreaks. The univariable logistic regression analysis identified several factors, including longer distance to federal highways, not short-cutting grass areas around stables, lack of dedicated facilities for carcass removal, and specific storage practices for feed, litter, and manure, as significantly associated with HPAI outbreak status. In the multivariable analysis, only the variables related to grass maintenance and carcass removal remained significant. The findings suggest that these biosecurity practices are critical in reducing HPAI risk, offering novel insights for improving surveillance and prevention strategies in poultry farming. The study's reliance on self-reported data and potential confounding variables limits its confidence, but the use of multivariable analysis provides a moderate level of evidence strength.

title: Human Infection with Avian Influenza A(H7N7) Virus, Taiwan, 2026

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the emergence of low pathogenic avian influenza A(H7N7) virus in humans and its potential for adaptation to mammalian hosts.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study focused on a poultry worker in Taiwan, 2026, who was infected with avian influenza A(H7N7) virus, and compared the virus to those circulating in Asian wild birds.
analysis.methods: The researchers characterized the virus through genetic analysis, identifying specific markers such as PB2 E627K associated with mammalian adaptation.
analysis.main_results: The virus isolated from the poultry worker was found to possess PB2 E627K, a marker indicating potential adaptation to mammalian hosts, and was related to viruses circulating in Asian wild birds.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that the avian influenza A(H7N7) virus detected in humans may have adapted to mammalian hosts, highlighting the need for further investigation into its zoonotic potential.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results emphasize the importance of monitoring avian influenza viruses in both poultry and wild bird populations to better understand their potential to infect humans and cause outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its focus on a single human case, but the genetic analysis provides moderate confidence in the identification of the virus's adaptation markers.

analysis.summary_en: This study reports a case of human infection with low pathogenic avian influenza A(H7N7) virus in Taiwan, 2026. The virus was found to be related to those circulating in Asian wild birds and possessed PB2 E627K, a marker associated with mammalian adaptation. The findings highlight the need for enhanced surveillance of avian influenza viruses in poultry and rapid characterization of human cases to assess pandemic potential. The study's focus on a single case limits the generalizability of the results, but the genetic analysis provides moderate confidence in the identification of adaptation markers. These results have implications for understanding the zoonotic potential of avian influenza viruses and the importance of monitoring their spread in both animal and human populations.

title: Antiviral Susceptibility of Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 and H5N5 Influenza Viruses Detected in Birds in Russia During 2021–2022

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to analyze the antiviral susceptibility of clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 and H5N5 influenza viruses detected in Russia during 2021–2022. The research addresses the need to understand antiviral resistance in avian influenza viruses, which is critical for effective treatment and control strategies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study investigated 40 avian influenza outbreaks in wild and domestic birds, isolating 109 H5N1 and 9 H5N5 strains during 2021–2022. These strains were collected from the European and Ural regions of Russia.
analysis.methods: A genetic approach was used to analyze markers associated with reduced susceptibility to baloxavir and M2 blockers, as well as markers of reduced inhibition by neuraminidase inhibitors (NAIs). Additionally, the isolated strains were tested in a functional assay to evaluate the inhibitory activity of oseltamivir, zanamivir, and peramivir against viral neuraminidase.
analysis.main_results: None of the tested strains demonstrated a ≥10-fold increase in NAI IC50 values compared to the corresponding subtype medians, and were thus classified as having a normal level of inhibition. title: Mice immunized with N1 neuraminidase in a single cycle infectious virus or in a recombinant nanoparticle vaccine are protected against lethal challenge with highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 influenza

analysis.research_question_and_background: The recent spillover of highly pathogenic (HP) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b into dairy cattle and other mammalian species has been concerning. Vaccine candidates that can be rapidly synthesized and implemented are key countermeasures for protecting the human population against emerging pathogens.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Here we examine the use of a pH1N1 virus lacking the genetic material for hemagglutinin (HA), limiting the infection to a single cycle (sciIAV) or Cobalt lipid-porphyrin nanoparticles decorated with neuraminidase (NA) of HPAI H5N1 (N1-CoPoP) as vaccine candidates.
analysis.methods: C57BL/6 mice were inoculated intranasally with a single dose of pH1N1 sciIAV or intramuscularly with N1-CoPoP alone or in combination with pH1N1 sciIAV. The study measured serum NA antibodies and viral titers in the lungs, nasal turbinates, and brain following lethal challenge with HPAIV H5N1.
analysis.main_results: C57BL/6 mice that were inoculated intranasally with a single dose of pH1N1 sciIAV did not differ in serum NA antibody compared to uninoculated mice. However, mice that were inoculated intramuscularly with the N1-CoPoP alone or in combination with pH1N1 sciIAV had increased N1 IgG antibodies.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Upon lethal challenge with HPAIV H5N1, all mice inoculated with either pH1N1 sciIAV or N1-CoPoP were protected from weight loss, unlike unvaccinated mice with substantial body weight losses that succumb to viral infection between 7 and 10 days post infection (dpi).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Both pH1N1 sciIAV and N1-CoPoP were protective and should be investigated further as alternative vaccine candidates.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations or evidence strength for the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the protective efficacy of two vaccine candidates against highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1. The research is motivated by the recent spillover of H5N1 into mammals and the need for rapid vaccine development. The study uses a pH1N1 virus lacking hemagglutinin (sciIAV) and Cobalt lipid-porphyrin nanoparticles decorated with neuraminidase (N1-CoPoP) to immunize mice. Results show that mice inoculated with N1-CoPoP alone or in combination with sciIAV had increased N1 IgG antibodies. Upon lethal challenge with HPAIV H5N1, all vaccinated mice were protected from weight loss, while unvaccinated mice experienced substantial weight loss and succumbed to infection. The findings suggest that both vaccine candidates are protective and warrant further investigation as alternatives for human use. The study does not report limitations or evidence strength, which may affect the confidence in its conclusions.

title: 2018–2025 Serological study on avian influenza among occupationally exposed populations in the Poyang Lake area — the region with the highest environmental surveillance positive rate in China

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to describe the seroprevalence of antibodies against selected avian influenza virus subtypes among occupationally exposed populations at surveillance sites around Poyang Lake from 2018 to 2025, and to provide data to inform ongoing surveillance and risk assessment.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional serological surveillance was conducted annually during winter and spring from 2018 to 2025 in Nanchang County (Nanchang) and Duchang and Wuning Counties (Jiujiang), Jiangxi Province.
analysis.methods: A total of 2,437 valid serum samples were analyzed (1,599 from Jiujiang and 838 from Nanchang).
analysis.main_results: During 2021–2025, 22 of 1,523 samples (1.44%) met the threshold for H3N8, including 9 of 100 samples (9.00%) collected in Nanchang in the 2024 surveillance year.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: During 2018–2020, 25 of 914 samples (2.74%) met the threshold for H7N9.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Continued serological surveillance, interpreted alongside poultry and environmental virological data, may inform risk assessment.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: HI reactivity alone does not establish subtype-specific human infection or local virus circulation.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to describe the seroprevalence of antibodies against selected avian influenza virus subtypes among occupationally exposed populations at surveillance sites around Poyang Lake from 2018 to 2025, and to provide data to inform ongoing surveillance and risk assessment. A cross-sectional serological surveillance was conducted annually during winter and spring from 2018 to 2025 in Nanchang County (Nanchang) and Duchang and Wuning Counties (Jiujiang), Jiangxi Province. A total of 2,437 valid serum samples were analyzed (1,599 from Jiujiang and 838 from Nanchang). During 2021–2025, 22 of 1,523 samples (1.44%) met the threshold for H3N8, including 9 of 100 samples (9.00%) collected in Nanchang in the 2024 surveillance year. During 2018–2020, 25 of 914 samples (2.74%) met the threshold for H7N9. Continued serological surveillance, interpreted alongside poultry and environmental virological data, may inform risk assessment. HI reactivity alone does not establish subtype-specific human infection or local virus circulation.

title: A review of fractional calculus models for avian influenza: Dynamics, memory effects, and control perspectives

analysis.scope_and_question: Avian influenza A viruses, avian-origin zoonotic infections, and qualified avian subtypes. Biologically related animal, taxonomic, model, differential-diagnosis and comparative entities are supplementary-only unless material target-specific evidence is also present; only explicit lexical or unrelated hard exclusions are terminal.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Based on the review of 16 studies combining fractional calculus with avian influenza or influenza transmission modeling, consistent evidence is provided that fractional-order models reproduce the real outbreak dynamics better than the classical ones.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: In this review, we have surveyed the use of fractional calculus in the modeling of avian influenza epidemics with emphasis on disease transmission, memory effects, and intervention strategies.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Key research gaps are identified, and future directions are proposed, including hybrid fractional-machine learning frameworks for real-time adaptive forecasting.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Avian influenza is a serious global public health threat, and both humans and animals can be infected.

analysis.summary_en: This review focuses on avian influenza A viruses and their implications for public health. It highlights the limitations of classical integer-order compartmental models in capturing the complex temporal dynamics of avian influenza outbreaks, particularly memory-dependent phenomena. The review emphasizes the use of fractional calculus in modeling avian influenza, with a focus on disease transmission, memory effects, and intervention strategies. It evaluates four fractional operators and their memory properties, noting that the Atangana-Baleanu-Caputo operator yields the fewest prediction errors in surveillance data. The review also identifies key research gaps, such as the need for hybrid fractional-machine learning frameworks for real-time adaptive forecasting. Overall, the findings suggest that fractional-order models offer improved accuracy in representing avian influenza dynamics compared to traditional models.

title: ARGUS: A Four-Signal Joint Model for H5N1 Neuraminidase Inhibitor Resistance Prediction

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the incompletely characterized resistance profiles of H5N1 influenza to oseltamivir and zanamivir, and the incompatibility of phenotypic screening timescales with clinical decision-making.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The research involved the development of ARGUS, a joint model combining four structural signals to predict H5N1 neuraminidase inhibitor resistance, using a comprehensive mutagenesis study and validation against published data.
analysis.methods: ARGUS integrated molecular docking affinity, protein language model evolutionary likelihood, perturbation response scanning, and all-atom pocket volume analysis to predict resistance.
analysis.main_results: The four-signal model achieved a leave-one-out Spearman ρ = 0.628 (p = 0.000032) with a 95% bootstrap interval of [0.428, 0.845] for in-sample correlation and a permutation p < 0.001. The model outperformed a two-signal linear blend on a smaller dataset.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: ARGUS provides immediate structural assessment of neuraminidase mutations without experimental work, and the full saturation landscape and trained models are publicly available.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: ARGUS can inform surveillance and treatment strategies for H5N1 influenza by predicting resistance patterns and guiding clinical decisions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of a non-randomized mutagenesis approach and the reliance on a specific set of structural signals, which may not generalize to all influenza subtypes.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed ARGUS, a joint model combining four structural signals to predict H5N1 neuraminidase inhibitor resistance, achieving a strong correlation with published data. ARGUS provides immediate structural assessment of mutations without experimental work, enhancing surveillance and treatment strategies.

title: Pathogenesis and Cross-species Potential of Emerging H3N3 Influenza Viruses with Mammalian-adaptive Mutations

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate the evolution, pathogenicity, and vaccine efficacy of emerging H3N3 avian influenza viruses with mammalian-adaptive mutations, as their emergence poses a threat to poultry and public health.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study characterized three novel H3N3 isolates (SQ2049, HN0120, and GT2125) from chickens in China, assessing their replicative fitness and pathogenicity in SPF chickens.
analysis.methods: Phylogenetic analysis was used to determine the origin of the isolates, and pathogenicity trials in SPF chickens evaluated their replication and shedding patterns. Additionally, mouse infection studies were conducted to identify HA substitutions associated with mammalian adaptation.
analysis.main_results: SQ2049 demonstrated efficient horizontal transmission in SPF chickens without clinical signs, with cloacal viral shedding persisting for 11 days and oral shedding lasting only 2 to 3 days. The inactivated SQ2049 vaccine elicited high cross-reactive antibody titers (HI≥8log2) and provided 100% protection in SPF chickens. GT2125 showed reduced efficiency in embryos and carried unique PB2 substitutions (V598I and K702).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings expand our understanding of H3N3 AIV evolutionary dynamics and highlight the importance of surveillance for reassortant influenza viruses, as the HA substitutions identified have previously been associated with mammalian adaptation and enhanced binding to human-type α-2,6 receptors.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The demonstrated vaccine efficacy provides a foundation for future H3N3 prevention and control strategies, and the study underscores the need for continued monitoring of avian influenza viruses with potential zoonotic capabilities.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to SPF chickens and mouse models, which may not fully represent natural host interactions. The evidence is moderate, as the functional effects of the HA substitutions in the H3N3 context were not evaluated.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the emergence of triple-reassortant H3N3 avian influenza viruses (AIVs) in China, focusing on their evolution, pathogenicity, and vaccine efficacy. Three novel isolates (SQ2049, HN0120, and GT2125) were characterized, revealing their origin from H10N3 and H3N8 lineages with an H9N2-derived internal gene backbone. SQ2049 showed efficient horizontal transmission in SPF chickens without clinical signs, with prolonged cloacal shedding and mild histopathological lesions. The inactivated SQ2049 vaccine elicited high cross-reactive antibody titers and provided complete protection. GT2125 exhibited reduced embryonic efficiency and unique PB2 substitutions. Mouse infection studies identified HA mutations linked to mammalian adaptation, though their functional effects in H3N3 were not assessed. These findings contribute to understanding H3N3 AIV dynamics and emphasize the importance of surveillance for reassortant viruses. The study highlights the potential for vaccine development against H3N3 AIVs but is limited to controlled models, suggesting moderate evidence strength.

title: Knowledge of Avian Influenza Among Poultry Workers & Development of SIM on Prevention of Avian Influenza

analysis.research_question_and_background: Avian influenza is an important zoonotic disease of global concern, with poultry workers at particular risk because of their close and frequent contact with birds and contaminated environments.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A descriptive cross‐sectional design was used, and 60 poultry workers were selected by simple random sampling from identified farms in the study area.
analysis.methods: Data were collected using a structured questionnaire consisting of demographic variables and 16 multiple‐choice items covering transmission, clinical manifestations in humans and birds, diagnosis, vaccination, biosecurity measures, safe cooking practices, and use of personal protective equipment.
analysis.main_results: The findings showed that 70% of poultry workers had average knowledge and 30% had good knowledge; none had bad or excellent knowledge. More than half of the workers reported no prior knowledge of avian influenza, and among those who had heard about it, the main sources were social media, newspapers, television, and health workers.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Important gaps were observed in the understanding of human‐to‐human transmission, recommended personal protective equipment, appropriate cooking practices, reporting of sick or dead birds, and farm‐level biosecurity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study highlights the need for simple, locally appropriate educational interventions to strengthen knowledge and promote safer practices among poultry workers, thereby reducing the risk of avian influenza transmission at the human–poultry interface.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Chi‐square analysis revealed no statistically significant association between knowledge level and selected demographic variables such as age, education, type of work, work experience, and previous knowledge.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to assess the level of knowledge regarding avian influenza among poultry workers in Sangli and Miraj city to develop a self-instructional module on prevention. A descriptive cross-sectional design was employed, involving 60 poultry workers selected through simple random sampling. Data were gathered using a structured questionnaire with 16 multiple-choice items covering various aspects of avian influenza. The results indicated that 70% of participants had average knowledge, while 30% had good knowledge, with no one achieving bad or excellent scores. Over half of the workers had no prior knowledge of avian influenza, and those who were aware primarily obtained information from social media, newspapers, television, and health workers. The study identified significant gaps in understanding key aspects of avian influenza, such as human-to-human transmission, personal protective equipment, cooking practices, and biosecurity measures. These findings underscore the importance of targeted educational interventions to improve knowledge and reduce transmission risks at the human-poultry interface. The study's limitations include the lack of a statistically significant association between knowledge levels and demographic factors, which may affect the generalizability of the results. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the study and the absence of control groups.

title: Territorial risk of high pathogenicity avian influenza in France is associated with farmed species diversity

analysis.research_question_and_background: Moreover, we show that the positive association between duck houses and HPAI risk weakens as the number of less-competent non-duck poultry houses increases, revealing a dilution effect within poultry production systems.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Animal infectious diseases threaten food security, livestock production and public health.
analysis.methods: Using spatial statistical models calibrated on three successive French high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) epidemics (2020-2023), we show that greater local diversity of livestock farms, including cattle and pig farms, is associated with significantly lower HPAI risk.
analysis.main_results: While disease prevention strategies typically target risk factors associated with high-competence hosts or environmental conditions, we hypothesise that lower-competence species can reduce disease risk by diluting effective contact rates between farms.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings suggest that livestock diversity is a previously overlooked determinant of disease spread and open new research avenues on territorial diversification to complement traditional approaches for the long-term control of high-impact animal infectious diseases.

title: Evidence of Exposure to Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza H5 Viruses in East Greenland Polar Bears

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to detect antibodies to highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in East Greenland polar bears, addressing the emerging threat of HPAI in Arctic ecosystems. The research fills a knowledge gap by identifying HPAI exposure in polar bears, which are apex predators in the Arctic and may serve as sentinels for viral spread.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved collecting heart blood samples from 109 polar bears during the hunting season (January–May) from 2016 to 2025. Samples were collected from East Greenland and analyzed for antibodies against influenza A viruses using a competitive ELISA and hemagglutination inhibition assay.
analysis.methods: Samples were screened for antibodies against all influenza A viruses using a competitive ELISA, and further testing was conducted using a hemagglutination inhibition assay with avian influenza viruses representative of H5 and H7 subtypes. The study complied with international permits for sample collection and transport.
analysis.main_results: Three bears from 2024 and six bears from 2025 had antibodies to HPAI, with signal-to-noise values within the positive range. Four of the six 2025 bears had antibodies to the highly pathogenic H5 clade 2.3.4.4b, indicating recent exposure.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study provides evidence of HPAI exposure in East Greenland polar bears, highlighting the need for increased surveillance in Arctic ecosystems. The findings suggest that polar bears may serve as sentinels for HPAI spread and emphasize the importance of collaboration between scientists and local subsistence hunters.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings caution that HPAI may pose a risk to Arctic species, including polar bears, and underscore the need for enhanced surveillance and monitoring of viral spread in these regions. The study also highlights the strength of collaboration between scientists and local hunters in monitoring wildlife health.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the small sample size and the potential for cross-reactivity with low pathogenic H5 subtypes. However, the findings are supported by the high prevalence of antibodies and the survival of the bears post-exposure, suggesting a strong evidence base.

analysis.summary_en: This study detected antibodies to highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in East Greenland polar bears, indicating recent exposure. The findings highlight the need for increased surveillance in Arctic ecosystems and emphasize the importance of collaboration between scientists and local hunters.

title: ATG13 Recruits LC3 to Target H9N2-IAV PB1 for Autophagic-Lysosomal Degradation and Restricts Viral Replication.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to elucidate the mechanism by which ATG13 modulates influenza A virus (IAV) replication, addressing the unclear role of ATG13 in this process.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved demonstrating the interaction between ATG13 and the viral polymerase basic protein 1 (PB1) of H9N2-IAV and the subsequent autophagic degradation of PB1.
analysis.methods: The study employed molecular biology techniques to demonstrate the interaction between ATG13 and PB1, and to investigate the autophagic degradation process.
analysis.main_results: ATG13 specifically interacts with the C-terminal domain of PB1 and recruits microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 (LC3) to promote the autophagolysosomal degradation of PB1, thereby suppressing viral replication.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This study reveals a novel mechanism whereby ATG13 negatively regulates IAV replication by mediating the targeted degradation of PB1 via the autophagolysosomal pathway.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide a potential therapeutic target for anti-influenza agents and unveil a new role of the autophagy pathway in host antiviral defense.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study does not provide a detailed description of the limitations and the strength of the evidence is not explicitly assessed.

analysis.summary_en: This study elucidated the mechanism by which ATG13 modulates influenza A virus (IAV) replication, demonstrating that ATG13 interacts with PB1 and promotes its autophagic degradation, thereby suppressing viral replication. The findings provide a potential therapeutic target for anti-influenza agents.
